cards.explanation: The two things are that God take His hand off Job and not terrify him. Job asks God to withdraw His hand and not let His terror frighten him (Job 13:21). If God grants them, Job says he won't need to hide from Him (Job 13:20). He wants to stand there and talk, not duck behind the furniture.

Job wants a chance to talk it out together. He says, “Then call me, and I will answer, or let me speak, and You can reply.” (Job 13:22) Either way, it goes back and forth. He isn't asking for a speech, friends. I think he wants a real conversation.

The word is enemy. Job asks, “Why do You hide Your face and consider me as Your enemy?” (Job 13:24) He asks it straight to God. Notice it comes out as a question, not a verdict. I think it's coming from a hurting place.

The answer is dry chaff. Job asks, “Would You frighten a windblown leaf? Would You chase after dry chaff?” (Job 13:25) Those are two light things that the wind pushes around. I think he's showing how small he feels. Nobody sprints after a leaf.

The answer is True. Job says to God, “For You record bitter accusations against me and bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth.” (Job 13:26) Bequeath is a fancy word for passing something down, like an inheritance. So Job feels like he's been handed a pile of old mistakes. I think that's a heavy thing to carry around.

The answer is wastes away. Job says man “…wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment.” (Job 13:28) Picture a coat with moth holes, slowly coming apart. That's the image he gives. It's about something wearing out, not something that happens in a flash.

The answer is False. Job says a person born of a woman is “…short of days…” and “…full of trouble.” (Job 14:1) Neither of those says long. He's describing a life as brief and hard. It's a heavy line, friends, and it's what the text says.

The word is withers. Job says, “Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away…” (Job 14:2) Picture a flower on the counter that looks great and then droops. Job uses that picture for a person's life. Up it comes, and then it fades.
The answer is False. Job asks who can bring out clean from unclean, then answers himself: “No one!” (Job 14:4) Effort never comes into it. The question has one answer.

Job asks God to look away and let him rest. He says, “…look away from him and let him rest…” (Job 14:6) This comes right after he says a man's days are determined and God has set limits he cannot exceed (Job 14:5). So he's asking for rest inside those limits. Even a hired hand gets a breather.

The answer is that it sprouts again. Job says, “If it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its tender shoots will not fail.” (Job 14:7) He calls that hope for a tree. Chop it down and it can come back. That's a tree with a real comeback story.

The answer is the scent of water. Job says, “…at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling.” (Job 14:9) Just a whiff, and the old stump gets going. I know folks who perk up at the scent of a fresh batch of cookies. Same energy.

The answer is False. Job lines up the tree and the man, then turns with “But a man dies and is laid low…” (Job 14:10) In verse 12 he says a man lies down and does not rise. He says that until the heavens are no more, the man will not be awakened. The tree and the man don't match in his picture.

The answer is that he wishes God would set a time and remember him. Job says, “If only You would appoint a time for me and then remember me!” (Job 14:13) So the wish has two parts: a set time, and then being remembered. He asks it of God and no one else. I think that's a hopeful thread in a heavy stretch.

The word is wait. Job says, “All the days of my hard service I will wait, until my renewal comes.” (Job 14:14) Wait. He doesn't say rush, and he doesn't say run. I once waited years in the back of a kitchen junk drawer, so I know waiting is no small thing.

The answer is True. Job says, “You will call, and I will answer; You will desire the work of Your hands.” (Job 14:15) He speaks of God desiring the work of His hands. After the heavy lines before it, this one lifts. It's a hopeful turn.

The word is sin. Job says, “For then You would count my steps, but would not keep track of my sin.” (Job 14:16) Steps get counted, but sin doesn't get tracked. Earlier he said God stands watch over all his paths (Job 13:27). I think this is a very different kind of watching.

The answer is that God would cover it over. Job says, “…You would cover over my iniquity.” (Job 14:17) He also says his transgression would be sealed in a bag. Both pictures are of sin tucked away, not put on display. I think it's a hopeful thing to hear from him.

The answer is that God destroys a man's hope. Job says, “…so You destroy a man’s hope.” (Job 14:19) Water wears away the stones and torrents wash away the soil, and he sets God's action beside those. This is a heavy line, friends. I think it comes from a painful place.

The answer is False. Job says, “If his sons receive honor, he does not know it; if they are brought low, he is unaware.” (Job 14:21) So honor or hardship for his sons, the man is unaware of both. This is Job describing it, and I think it comes from a sad place. It's a heavy verse.

The word is body. Job says, “He feels only the pain of his own body and mourns only for himself.” (Job 14:22) So the pain he names is in the body. It's the last verse of this stretch, and I think it ends on a lonely note. Job is wrapping up a heavy thought.
